newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvian balanced budget plans thrown into doubt.
newsitem.headline: Latvian balanced budget plans thrown into doubt.

text.p: Latvian Finance Minister Roberts Zile on Thursday said the country's goal of a balanced budget for 1997 was in jeopardy as income tax revenues would probably fall short of target.
Zile told a news conference that the budget deficit could reach around 10 million lats ($17.1 million) or 0.4 percent of the Baltic state's gross domestic product.
"If income tax and value-added tax collection...does not improve drastically during the rest of the year, we might face a slight deficit," Zile said.
"We are still close to zero when we balance the real income with the planned expenditure."
He said high-ranking officials had been "manipulating the figures" but mentioned no names.
The government had originally targeted a balanced budget and the figures to date suggested that goal was on track.
Outgoing Prime Minister Andris Shkele, who resigned on Monday after several ministers stood down over corruption allegations, said that the budget was in surplus.

Shkele, a no-nonsense businessman with no party affiliations, was credited with bringing order to public finances and quickening the pace of reforms launched when the country quit the Soviet Union in 1991.
But Zile said that the 35 million lat surplus could be run down by 31 million lats in public sector expenditures which had been allocated but not spent yet.
Planned budget expenditure for the first half of 1997 were 284.59 million lats and the actual figure came to 252.99 million lats, Zile said.
Dealers said a modest deficit was unlikely to have a big impact on the country's domestic debt market, which has witnessed a steady decline in yields on Treasury bills.
"If there is a deficit, it won't have much affect on T-bill rates, unless the government brings more paper to the market to fill the shortfall," said one local debt dealer.
-- Martinsh Gravitis, Riga newsroom +371 722 66 93 ($ = 0.584 Latvian Lats)
